## 7.5 Does the *animacy* judgment depend on acoustic cues?

These two models flip the perception outcome from "big" to "animate" and ask whether listeners draw on vowel duration or f0 to decide whether they are hearing an animal. Treating animacy as an outcome here is sound-symbolism in the broader sense: the same acoustic dimensions that encode size might also leak into the animate/inanimate distinction.

```{r rq4, results='hide'}
m_anim_dur <- fit_perc_bin("animate_judgment", "vowel_dur_ms_mean_z")
m_anim_f0  <- fit_perc_bin("animate_judgment", "f0_mean_z")
```

```{r expl-anim-display-dur, fig.height=3, fig.cap=capFig("Perception: vowel duration as cue to animacy judgment.")}
summary(m_anim_dur)
pp_check(m_anim_dur, ndraws = 100) + ggtitle("PPC – vowel duration → animate judgment")
```

```{r expl-anim-display-f0, fig.height=3, fig.cap=capFig("Perception: f0 as cue to animacy judgment.")}
summary(m_anim_f0)
pp_check(m_anim_f0, ndraws = 100) + ggtitle("PPC – f0 → animate judgment")
```

## 7.6 A note on multinomial category judgments

A logical extension would be to model the full 6-way `picked_category` outcome (bird, mammal, reptile, appliance, vehicle, instrument) as a multinomial response to the same acoustic cues. We considered this and decided against including it in the main analysis for two reasons. First, a categorical 6-level outcome multiplies the coefficient space (5 contrasts × every fixed effect) and is hard to summarize compactly in a short-format paper. Second, it does not speak directly to our expectations: the size question is covered by §6, and the animacy question is covered by §6 (for animacy as production-side baseline) and §7.5 (for animacy as a perceptual outcome on its own). The chunk below is left in the script for transparency – it can be turned on by setting `eval=TRUE` – but is not part of the reported analysis. The model also does not add a parallel f0 version because the animacy-judgment perception model in §7.5 already captures the relevant question for that channel.

```{r rq3, eval=FALSE, results='hide'}
m_cat_dur <- fit_brm(
  bf(picked_category ~ vowel_dur_ms_mean_z * animacy_c +
       (1 | listener) + (1 | speaker) + (1 | item_english)),
  data   = perc |> filter(!is.na(vowel_dur_ms_mean_z)) |>
                   mutate(picked_category = factor(picked_category)),
  family = categorical(),
  file   = paste0(models, "m_cat_dur")
)
```

## 7.7 Exploratory takeaways

These results are read as descriptive flags, not robust findings, and we mark the directions
that look worth following up.

**Vocalic features beyond duration and f0.** F1 is credibly lower for big referents on the log scale (β = -0.06, 95% HDI [-0.10, -0.03]; ~6% lower F1 for big). Mechanistically a lower F1 can come from either a less open mouth or a higher tongue position (the two move together but not one-to-one), so the direction is at face value the *opposite* of the open-vowel-for-big
stereotype – our speakers are realizing big referents with a slightly more closed or
higher-tongue vocalic gesture, not a more open one. The direction also runs against
@cwiek_scope_2025's null on lip opening and formant dispersion for object size, but the
paradigms differ enough (their participants "shot" at cans of different sizes on the wall
while saying *piff* or *paff*; ours imitatively portrayed both animate and inanimate
referents in a carrier sentence) that we treat the contrast as hypothesis-generating rather
than as evidence against their conclusion. F2 shows no credible size effect. CPP is
credibly higher for big referents (β = 1.10 dB, 95% HDI [0.11, 2.11]),
consistent with more periodic voicing for big-referent productions, and credibly
lower for animate referents (animacy main effect β = -1.57, 95% HDI [-2.44, -0.69]) –
with the same caveat as in §7.8: the animacy main effect on any of these channels
may reflect item-level dimensions that travel with the animate/inanimate split
rather than animacy as a feature. H1–H2 is also credibly lower for big referents (β = −1.21 dB, 95% HDI [−2.31, −0.11]) – with CPP, a converging hint that big-referent productions carry a less breathy, more pressed voice.
On the perception side, listeners used neither CPP (β = −0.09, 95% HDI [−0.27, 0.09]) nor H1–H2 (β = 0.03, 95% HDI [−0.15, 0.21]) to judge size: the voice-quality channel, like vowel duration, is produced here but not decoded.

**Fricative production.** Fricative SPL is louder for big referents by roughly 3 dB
(β = 3.08, 95% HDI [0.61, 5.61]) – the clearest iconic effect among the fricative measures.
Fricative duration is in the size-iconic direction but its 95% HDI brushes zero (β = 0.10,
95% HDI [-0.02, 0.21]; P(β > 0) ≈ 0.95). Fricative peak frequency and centre of gravity show
no credible size effect; phoneme identity, as expected, dominates both.

**Fricative perception.** Listeners use fricative duration as a cue to size
(β = 0.25, 95% HDI [0.04, 0.45]) and the use is amplified for animate referents
(interaction β = 0.50, 95% HDI [0.09, 0.91]). Listeners also use fricative SPL
(β = 0.24, 95% HDI [0.05, 0.43]). F1, F2, fricative peak frequency, and fricative centre of gravity are not credibly used.
The fricative-duration result is interesting on its own: it is a perception-side effect for a
production-side feature whose production-side credibility was marginal – a pattern more often
seen the other way round in this dataset.

**Animacy judgment.** Listeners judge productions as animate more often when speaker f0 is
higher (β = 0.23 log-odds per +1 SD, 95% HDI [0.01, 0.45]; OR ≈ 1.26). The corresponding
duration model is null (β = -0.10, 95% HDI [-0.28, 0.09]). The interaction with portrayed
animacy in the f0 model is suggestive but its HDI crosses zero (β = 0.41, 95% HDI [-0.03, 0.87]).
The pattern is consistent with f0 carrying both a size signal (lower f0 → bigger) and an
animacy signal (higher f0 → animate), and the two are dissociable in the data.

## 7.8 Cuteness as a candidate explanation for the animacy main effect

The §6 finding that animate referents are produced with shorter vowels and
higher f0 *regardless of their size* is striking but interpretively
ambiguous: the animal stimuli differ from the object stimuli on more than
just animacy. One obvious candidate is **perceived cuteness**: a separate
group of 17 raters scored each stimulus picture for cuteness on a 1–7 scale.
Cuteness covaries with animacy (animals tend to be rated cuter than
appliances and vehicles) and partly with size (smaller things tend to be
cuter than bigger things), so it is a plausible carrier of what the §6
animacy main effect is picking up.

We test this in the same way the original animacy main effect was tested:
refit each of the four primary-claim models *plus* the animate-judgment
perception model from §7.5, adding `cuteness_z` (z-scored per-item mean
cuteness) as a fixed effect alongside `size_c * animacy_c`. The question
is descriptive: does the animacy coefficient shrink toward zero when
cuteness is partialled out, and does cuteness itself carry a credible
effect on each outcome?

The random-effects structure is unchanged. Cuteness varies only between
items, so it does not enter as a varying slope at the speaker or listener
level – the `(1 | item_english)` intercept still absorbs the
between-item residual after cuteness is accounted for.

### 7.8.1 Augmented production models

```{r m-cute-prod, results='hide'}
m_vdur_cute <- fit_brm(
  bf(vowel_dur_ms ~ size_c * animacy_c + cuteness_z + vowel +
       (1 + size_c | speaker) + (1 | item_english)),
  data   = vowel_long |> filter(!is.na(vowel_dur_ms), !is.na(cuteness_z)),
  family = lognormal(),
  file   = paste0(models, "m_vdur_cute")
)

m_f0_cute <- fit_brm(
  bf(f0 ~ size_c * animacy_c + cuteness_z + sex + vowel +
       (1 + size_c | speaker) + (1 | item_english)),
  data   = vowel_long |> filter(!is.na(f0), !is.na(cuteness_z)),
  family = lognormal(),
  file   = paste0(models, "m_f0_cute")
)
```

```{r m-cute-prod-display}
summary(m_vdur_cute)
summary(m_f0_cute)
```

### 7.8.2 Augmented perception models

```{r m-cute-perc, results='hide'}
m_perc_f0_cute <- fit_brm(
  bf(big_judgment ~ f0_mean_z * animacy_c + cuteness_z +
       (1 | listener) + (1 | speaker) + (1 | item_english)),
  data   = perc |> filter(!is.na(f0_mean_z), !is.na(cuteness_z)),
  family = bernoulli(),
  file   = paste0(models, "m_perc_f0_cute")
)

m_anim_f0_cute <- fit_brm(
  bf(animate_judgment ~ f0_mean_z * animacy_c + cuteness_z +
       (1 | listener) + (1 | speaker) + (1 | item_english)),
  data   = perc |> filter(!is.na(f0_mean_z), !is.na(cuteness_z)),
  family = bernoulli(),
  file   = paste0(models, "m_anim_f0_cute")
)
```

```{r m-cute-perc-display}
summary(m_perc_f0_cute)
summary(m_anim_f0_cute)
```

### 7.8.3 Directional tests on the cuteness coefficient

```{r m-cute-effects}
report_effect(m_vdur_cute,    "cuteness_z", direction = "auto",
              label = "Cuteness → vowel duration (production)")
report_effect(m_f0_cute,      "cuteness_z", direction = "auto",
              label = "Cuteness → f0 (production)")
report_effect(m_perc_f0_cute, "cuteness_z", direction = "auto",
              label = "Cuteness → 'big' judgment (perception, f0 model)")
report_effect(m_anim_f0_cute, "cuteness_z", direction = "auto",
              label = "Cuteness → 'animate' judgment (perception, f0 model)")

# And the animacy main effect in each augmented model – the comparison number
report_effect(m_vdur_cute,    "animacy_c", direction = "auto",
              label = "Animacy main effect on vowel duration AFTER controlling for cuteness")
report_effect(m_f0_cute,      "animacy_c", direction = "auto",
              label = "Animacy main effect on f0 AFTER controlling for cuteness")
report_effect(m_perc_f0_cute, "animacy_c", direction = "auto",
              label = "Animacy main effect on 'big' judgment AFTER controlling for cuteness")
report_effect(m_anim_f0_cute, "animacy_c", direction = "auto",
              label = "Animacy main effect on 'animate' judgment AFTER controlling for cuteness")
```

### 7.8.4 Side-by-side: animacy posterior with and without cuteness

This is the visual that answers the question. For each outcome, we overlay
the posterior of the animacy main-effect coefficient from the baseline
model (§§6.2–6.5, §7.5) and from the cuteness-augmented model (§§7.8.1–2).
If cuteness is doing the work the animacy main effect was credited for in
§6, the augmented posterior should shrink toward zero relative to the
baseline.

```{r animacy-shift, fig.height=5.5, dpi=600, fig.retina=1, fig.width=9, fig.cap=capFig("Animacy main-effect posterior in the baseline model vs. the cuteness-augmented model. Shrinkage toward zero indicates that cuteness absorbs the animacy effect.")}
extract_animacy <- function(model, outcome_name, model_kind) {
  as_draws_df(model) |>
    transmute(outcome    = outcome_name,
              model_kind = model_kind,
              value      = b_animacy_c)
}

animacy_compare <- bind_rows(
  extract_animacy(m_vdur,         "vowel duration (production, log)", "baseline"),
  extract_animacy(m_vdur_cute,    "vowel duration (production, log)", "+ cuteness"),
  extract_animacy(m_f0,           "f0 (production, log)",             "baseline"),
  extract_animacy(m_f0_cute,      "f0 (production, log)",             "+ cuteness"),
  extract_animacy(m_perc_f0,      "f0 → big judgment (logit)",        "baseline"),
  extract_animacy(m_perc_f0_cute, "f0 → big judgment (logit)",        "+ cuteness"),
  extract_animacy(m_anim_f0,      "f0 → animate judgment (logit)",    "baseline"),
  extract_animacy(m_anim_f0_cute, "f0 → animate judgment (logit)",    "+ cuteness")
) |>
  mutate(
    outcome    = factor(outcome,    levels = unique(outcome)),
    model_kind = factor(model_kind, levels = c("baseline", "+ cuteness"))
  )

ggplot(animacy_compare,
       aes(x = value, y = fct_rev(outcome), fill = model_kind)) +
  stat_halfeye(
    .width         = c(0.66, 0.95),
    alpha          = 0.85,
    slab_colour    = "white",       # fixed, not mapped — kills the 2nd legend
    slab_linewidth = 0.3,
    position       = position_dodge(width = 0.65)
  ) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = 2, colour = "grey40") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = colorBlindBlack8[c(3, 7)]) +
  labs(
    x        = "Animacy main-effect estimate (link scale)",
    y        = NULL,
    fill     = NULL#,
    #title    = "Does cuteness absorb the animacy main effect?",
    #subtitle = "Each outcome: baseline model (§6 / §7.5) vs. with cuteness_z added"
  ) +
  theme(
    plot.title          = element_text(size = 13, face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle       = element_text(size = 10, colour = "grey30"),
    plot.title.position = "plot",          # lets title use the full plot width
    legend.position     = "top",
    legend.justification = "left",
    axis.text.y         = element_text(size = 10.5),
    axis.title.x        = element_text(size = 10.5),
    panel.grid.minor    = element_blank()
  )
```

### 7.8.5 Cuteness posterior across the five augmented models

```{r cute-forest, fig.height=3.5, fig.cap=capFig("Cuteness coefficient across the five augmented models. Production outcomes are on the log scale; perception outcomes are on the logit scale.")}
cute_forest <- bind_rows(
  extract_term(m_vdur_cute,    "cuteness_z", "vowel duration (production, log)"),
  extract_term(m_f0_cute,      "cuteness_z", "f0 (production, log)"),
  extract_term(m_perc_f0_cute, "cuteness_z", "f0 → big judgment (logit)"),
  extract_term(m_anim_f0_cute, "cuteness_z", "f0 → animate judgment (logit)")
) |>
  mutate(model = factor(model, levels = unique(model)))

ggplot(cute_forest, aes(x = value, y = fct_rev(model))) +
  stat_halfeye(.width = c(0.66, 0.95)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = 2, colour = "grey40") +
  labs(x = "Cuteness coefficient (per +1 SD item cuteness)",
       y = NULL,
       title = "Effect of perceived cuteness across outcomes")
```

### 7.8.6 Reading

**Production: animacy shrinks, but cuteness doesn't replace it.** The
animacy main effect on both production outcomes shrinks toward zero when
cuteness enters the model. On vowel duration, the baseline coefficient
(β = −0.15, 95% HDI [−0.28, −0.02]) becomes β = −0.07 [−0.38, 0.22] –
the point estimate halves and the HDI widens to straddle zero. On f0,
the baseline coefficient (β = +0.10, 95% HDI [0.00, 0.20]) becomes
β = +0.02 [−0.19, 0.24]. But the cuteness coefficient does *not* take
over the variance the animacy effect lost: cuteness on duration is
β = −0.04 [−0.20, 0.11] (P(β < 0) = 0.71) and cuteness on f0 is
β = +0.05 [−0.07, 0.17] (P(β > 0) = 0.79). Neither predictor reaches
credibility in the augmented models.

The cleanest read is that animacy and cuteness are too tightly correlated
in this stimulus set (§3.4 already shows that animals are systematically
cuter than objects) to be separately identified from 36 items' worth of
between-item variance. The §6 animacy main effect on production is
therefore fragile under any item-level covariate that tracks the
animal-vs-object distinction; we cannot tell from the present data
whether the carrier is animacy *qua* feature, cuteness, or a third
item-level dimension confounded with both.

**Perception: a different pattern – suppressor-style instability rather
than absorption.** The big-judgment model behaves unusually when cuteness
enters. The baseline animacy coefficient (β = −0.92, 95% HDI
[−2.18, 0.36], P = 0.93) flips sign and inflates to β = +2.28
[0.68, 3.99], P = 0.998, while the cuteness coefficient becomes large
and negative (β = −1.83 [−2.70, −0.98]; OR = 0.16; P > 0.999) and the f0
effect itself is essentially unchanged (β = −0.52 [−0.77, −0.26]). An
animacy posterior that grows *and* flips sign while a correlated covariate
enters with a large opposite-sign coefficient is a classical suppressor
pattern: the two predictors are jointly identifying a contrast that
neither captures alone, and the individual coefficients on that contrast
cannot be interpreted as effects of animacy or of cuteness on their own.
We do not read a substantive claim off this fit.

The animate-judgment model is, by contrast, almost untouched by adding
cuteness: animacy stays at β ≈ +2.2 in both baseline and augmented fits,
and cuteness is null (β = −0.09 [−0.71, 0.49]). This is the expected
pattern when the outcome and a fixed effect index nearly the same thing –
listeners judge animals as animate from the picture, and there is
correspondingly little residual room for an item-level cuteness covariate
to add explanatory value.

**The §6 size effects are unaffected.** A useful side check from the
augmented production models: the size effect on vowel duration
(β = +0.14 [−0.03, 0.30]) and on f0 (β = −0.16 [−0.28, −0.04]) barely
move from their §6 values (+0.16 and −0.18 respectively), and the
perception-of-f0 effect (β = −0.52) is unchanged. The primary §6 claims
– that speakers reliably lengthen vowels and lower f0 for big referents,
and that listeners use f0 to call "big" – are therefore not contaminated
by item-level cuteness or animacy. Size iconicity rides on top of these
between-item dimensions, not through them.

**Bottom line for the §6 animacy story.** The cuteness analysis does not
cleanly support the §6 reading of an animacy main effect, but it also
does not cleanly support a "cuteness in disguise" alternative. What it
does support is the limitation already flagged in §9: in this stimulus
set, animacy is confounded with item-level dimensions (cuteness being
one we can name) to a degree that the present design cannot resolve.
The honest write-up is to keep §6 as a descriptive observation –
animate referents in this set were produced with shorter vowels and
higher f0, and listener big-judgments tracked f0 – without claiming
animacy *qua* feature as the carrier of the production-side baseline
shift. A design that orthogonalises animacy and cuteness, with more
items per cell, would be needed to identify either independently.

# 8. Cross-feature comparison

The three forest plots below give the visual synthesis of §§6–7. The first asks where size leaks
into the produced signal across all ten acoustic features we measured. The second asks which of
those features listeners use to judge size. The third looks at the same question for animacy
judgments instead of size judgments. Each panel is on its own scale (log multiplicative effects,
dB, Hz, or log-odds) – the comparisons within a panel are meaningful; the comparisons across
panels are not.

## 8.1 Production: where does size leak into the signal?

```{r forest-prod, fig.height=9, dpi=600, fig.retina=1, fig.cap=capFig("Production: size effect across all acoustic features, faceted by effect-size scale (log, dB, Hz). Each panel has its own x-axis range – magnitudes across panels are NOT directly comparable.")}
forest_prod <- bind_rows(
  extract_term(m_vdur,  "size_c", "vowel duration (log)"),
  extract_term(m_f0,    "size_c", "f0 (log)"),
  extract_term(m_F1,    "size_c", "F1 (log)"),
  extract_term(m_F2,    "size_c", "F2 (log)"),
  extract_term(m_fdur,  "size_c", "fricative duration (log)"),
  extract_term(m_CPP,   "size_c", "CPP (dB)"),
  extract_term(m_H1H2,  "size_c", "H1–H2 (dB)"),
  extract_term(m_fSPL,  "size_c", "fricative SPL (dB)"),
  extract_term(m_fpeak, "size_c", "fricative peak (Hz)"),
  extract_term(m_fCoG,  "size_c", "fricative CoG (Hz)")
) |>
  mutate(
    scale_group = case_when(
      str_detect(model, "\\(log\\)") ~ "Log scale (lognormal models)",
      str_detect(model, "\\(dB\\)")  ~ "dB scale (Gaussian)",
      str_detect(model, "\\(Hz\\)")  ~ "Hz scale (Gaussian)"
    ),
    scale_group = factor(scale_group,
                         levels = c("Log scale (lognormal models)",
                                    "dB scale (Gaussian)",
                                    "Hz scale (Gaussian)")),
    model = factor(model, levels = unique(model))
  )

ggplot(forest_prod, aes(x = value, y = fct_rev(model))) +
  stat_halfeye(.width = c(0.66, 0.95)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = 2, colour = "grey40") +
  facet_wrap(~ scale_group, scales = "free", ncol = 1) +
  labs(x = "Effect of big vs. small (sum-coded)",
       y = NULL#,
       #title = "Production: size effect across all acoustic features",
       #subtitle = "Top panel includes the primary-claim outcomes (vowel duration, f0)"
       )
```
 
## 8.2 Perception: which cues drive "big" judgments?

```{r forest-perc, fig.height=4, dpi=600, fig.retina=1, fig.cap=capFig("Perception: log-odds shift in 'big' judgment per +1 SD of each acoustic feature. Top two rows = primary claim; below = exploratory.")}
forest_perc <- bind_rows(
  extract_term(m_perc_dur,   "vowel_dur_ms_mean_z", "vowel duration"),
  extract_term(m_perc_f0,    "f0_mean_z",           "f0"),
  extract_term(m_perc_F1,    "F1_mean_z",           "F1"),
  extract_term(m_perc_F2,    "F2_mean_z",           "F2"),
  extract_term(m_perc_CPP,   "CPP_mean_z",          "CPP"),
  extract_term(m_perc_H1H2,  "H1H2_mean_z",         "H1–H2"),
  extract_term(m_perc_fCoG,  "fric_CoG_Hz_mean_z",  "fricative CoG"),
  extract_term(m_perc_fdur,  "fric_dur_ms_mean_z",  "fricative duration"),
  extract_term(m_perc_fSPL,  "fric_SPL_dB_mean_z",  "fricative SPL"),
  extract_term(m_perc_fpeak, "fric_peak_Hz_mean_z", "fricative peak")
) |>
  mutate(model = factor(model, levels = unique(model)))

ggplot(forest_perc, aes(x = value, y = fct_rev(model))) +
  stat_halfeye(.width = c(0.66, 0.95)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = 2, colour = "grey40") +
  labs(x = "log-odds shift of \"big\" judgment per +1 SD acoustic feature",
       y = NULL#,
       #title = "Perception: which cues drive \"big\" judgments?",
       #subtitle = "Top two rows = primary claim; below = exploratory"
       )
```

## 8.3 Perception: which cues drive "animate" judgments?

```{r forest-anim, fig.height=2.5, fig.cap=capFig("Perception: log-odds shift in 'animate' judgment per +1 SD of speaker vowel duration or f0.")}
forest_anim <- bind_rows(
  extract_term(m_anim_dur, "vowel_dur_ms_mean_z", "vowel duration"),
  extract_term(m_anim_f0,  "f0_mean_z",           "f0")
) |>
  mutate(model = factor(model, levels = unique(model)))

ggplot(forest_anim, aes(x = value, y = fct_rev(model))) +
  stat_halfeye(.width = c(0.66, 0.95)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = 2, colour = "grey40") +
  labs(x = "log-odds shift of \"animate\" judgment per +1 SD acoustic feature",
       y = NULL,
       title = "Perception: which cues drive \"animate\" judgments?")
```

# 9. Discussion and limitations

The data support a partly asymmetric picture of size iconicity. On the production side, both
predicted channels work – speakers reliably lengthen vowels and lower f0 for big referents.
On the perception side only f0 closes the loop: listeners rely on f0 to call "big", but they
do not use vowel duration even though speakers reliably produce it. The duration channel is
production-only in this dataset. This asymmetry is the kind of pattern a pluripotential view of
iconic features would predict (different speakers and different listeners can recruit different
acoustic channels to convey or recover the same semantic dimension), but a directed replication
would be needed to take it as more than suggestive.

Animacy entered the production models as a main effect rather than as a modulator
of the size effect: animate referents in this stimulus set were produced with
shorter vowels and higher f0 regardless of their size, with the size effect itself
essentially unchanged across the animate/inanimate split. We treat this as a
descriptive observation rather than as evidence for animacy qua feature.
A separately-collected per-item cuteness rating (§7.8) provides the cleanest
available diagnostic: when cuteness is added as a covariate to the production
models, the animacy main effect shrinks toward zero, but cuteness itself does
not take its place – both predictors become non-credible. The honest read is
that animals and objects in this stimulus set differ acoustically in ways that
go beyond their size, but that the 36-item design lacks the resolution to
identify which item-level dimension is responsible. Listeners' "animate"
judgments, separately, are modulated by speaker f0 (§7.5), and this perception
pattern survives the cuteness control (§7.8) unchanged.

The exploratory channels are descriptive: CPP and F1 in production, and fricative duration and
fricative SPL in perception, all show credible effects that are worth a closer look in a
study designed around them. We flag them rather than claim them.

Three limitations are worth naming. (i) The stimulus set is small (36 items) and confounds
size with referent identity – speaker-level random effects help but cannot fully partial this
out. (ii) Listeners had a picture in front of them, so item identity is the dominant driver
of any judgment; the acoustic cues modulate on top of an already strong prior (see the
item-level baselines in §6.7). (iii) Animacy is confounded with item-level dimensions of the stimulus set – a
separately-collected cuteness rating (§7.8) is one such dimension, and likely
not the only one – to a degree that the present 36-item design cannot resolve.
A design that orthogonalises animacy and cuteness (and ideally other item-level
dimensions that travel with the animal/object split, such as baseline
expressiveness or articulatory complexity), with more items per cell, would be
needed to identify animacy as a semantic feature in production.
